paras: The lynching of Herman and Irvin Arthur was the burning of two Black brothers by a white mob at Paris, Lamar County, Texas, on July 6, 1920, after they were accused of killing a white farmer and his son. A special grand jury indicted five persons for first-degree murder, but no report of an arrest or trial appears in the coverage. Black newspapers covered it first through the indictments and then through a Paris resident's letter released by the NAACP.

According to the Paris resident's letter, the Arthurs were tenants working "on halves" for a white landlord named Hodges, who demanded they work all day Saturday. When they refused to work past noon, he threw their dinner and household goods into the yard while his son held a gun on them, and took their clothes on the claim that they owed him.

While the two brothers were loading a truck, Hodges and his son arrived. Both the letter and Mrs. Arthur said the Hodgeses fired first and that one brother, Herman in the letter, returned fire and killed both men.

The letter said the brothers' three sisters were in jail "on the pretence of protection" and were beaten for screaming while the mob took their brothers from the jail. The brothers were burned at stakes at the fair grounds, in daylight and before hundreds of people, according to the Chicago Defender and the Chicago Whip. A Defender correspondent added that the school superintendent and ministers urged the crowd on and that photographs of the mob sold the next day for a nickel.

Afterward the bodies were dragged through the streets where Black residents lived in a parade of 17 cars and a truck, with white men calling on them to "come out and see them and take warning." The letter writer said the sisters, aged 20, 17 and 14, were then stripped and assaulted in the jail basement by officers and twenty other white men and made to leave town.

The next day, the Tulsa Star reported, the county sheriff said "at least one of the two was not the right one," and Governor W. P. Hobby answered an NAACP protest by saying that Texas needed no "suggestions from the outside." In early August a special grand jury reported five indictments for first-degree murder, though many witnesses could not identify any ringleaders; the Chicago Whip described the five as white men. A later dispatch said they would be tried at the next term of court; in September the Cleveland Advocate wrote that not one of the lynchers had been brought to justice.

The surviving family, Scott Arthur, 70, his wife and their children, fled to Chicago, where Dr. W. W. Lucas met them at the Polk Street station. Black residents of Paris had raised their fares, the Defender reported, and the paper opened a relief fund. The letter writer said hundreds of Black residents had left Paris since the lynching.

No white-press report of the lynching or the indictments appears in the August and September coverage. The first Black-press reports, in early August, were an Associated Negro Press dispatch on the grand jury, headlined "Grand Jury Indicts Five Texas Lynchers" in the Cleveland Advocate and reprinted by the Negro Star, the Black Dispatch and the Savannah Tribune. The Chicago Whip called the burning a "peculiar southern sport," and the Tulsa Star set Hobby against governors who had protected prisoners from mobs.

A second wave followed in September, when the NAACP released the Paris letter, headlined by the New York Age "How Arthur Boys Were Lynched And Three Young Sisters Raped." The Cleveland Advocate, the Baltimore Afro-American and the Cleveland Gazette printed it too, and the Advocate's editorial "They Dared to Protect Their Own" recast the brothers as defenders of their family.

The NAACP dated the lynching July 6 and the Defender July 8, and the brothers' ages appear as 18 and 28 in the Defender but 19 and 22 in the Afro-American. The ANP wire said the brothers were held for murdering "a farmer and his son" and the Tulsa Star said "two white men," while the letter writer and Mrs. Arthur said Hodges and his son fired first.

reader.title: Lynching of Herman and Irvin Arthur
bases: A mob took two Black brothers held on a murder charge and burned them at stakes at Paris, Texas (A5, A15, A27).

Two Black men accused of killing a white farmer and his son were burned to death by a mob before hundreds of people, with no lawful authority, and five persons were later indicted for murder (A4, A5, A6, A27).

The ANP grand-jury dispatch (A5), the Tulsa Star editorial (A6), the NAACP's Paris letter (A27, A21) and Mrs. Arthur's interview (A19) independently report the burning of two Black men at Paris; no white-press report was found.

accounts.label: ANP wire (grand jury)
accounts.gist: Two Black men held for murdering a farmer and his son were burned; a special grand jury returned five first-degree murder indictments but witnesses could not identify ringleaders.

accounts.label: Paris resident's letter (NAACP)
accounts.gist: After a dispute over Saturday work, Hodges and his son fired on the brothers as they loaded a truck, and Herman killed both; a mob took the brothers from jail, burned them, paraded the bodies, and officers and white men assaulted the sisters in jail.

accounts.label: Mrs. Viola Arthur
accounts.gist: Hodges broke down the door and he and his son shot at her sons, and her veteran son returned fire, killing both.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender
accounts.gist: The sons were burned at stakes at the fair grounds on July 8 after killing a white man who tried to kill their father; the daughters were jailed.

accounts.label: County sheriff (via Tulsa Star)
accounts.gist: The day after, the sheriff said at least one of the two burned was not the right man.

framing.detail: Chicago Whip: 'peculiar southern sport', 'two innocent men', predicts no conviction.
Tulsa Star editorial contrasts Hobby with governors who protected prisoners.
ANP grand-jury dispatch run with headlines such as 'Grand Jury Indicts Five Texas Lynchers'.
New York Age: 'How Arthur Boys Were Lynched And Three Young Sisters Raped'; Gazette: 'Unspeakable Brutality'.
Cleveland Advocate editorial 'They Dared to Protect Their Own' stresses the veteran and the absence of justice.
Chicago Defender: "'Armenia' Outdone by White Cannibals in Paris, Texas"; relief fund; attacks a local minister as a traitor.
